title: CCPR/C/145/D/3167/2028-3218/2028
text: CCPR/C/145/D/3167/2018CCPR/C/145/D/3218/2018Advance unedited versionDistr.: General30 March 2026Original: EnglishHuman Rights CommitteeViews adopted by the Committee under the Optional Protocol, concerning communications Nos. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018*,**Communication submitted by:Johan Lets Pretorius, Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius (represented by Hercules Booysen) Alleged victims:The authorsState Party:South AfricaDate of communications:31 January and 22 July 2018 (initial submissions)Document references:Decisions taken pursuant to rule 92 of the Committee’s rules of procedure, transmitted to the State party on 27 March 2018 and 3 December 2018 (not issued in document form) Date of adoption of Views:10 March 2026Subject matter:Fair trial; undue delay in proceedings; lack of legal representation; right to reviewProcedural issues:Exhaustion of domestic remedies; level of substantiation of claimsSubstantive issues:Arbitrary arrest or detention; conditions of detention; right to liberty of movement; right to fair trial; right to privacy; non-discriminationArticles of the Covenant:9 (1), 10 (3), 12 (1-2), 14 (1-2), (3b-e) and (5), 17 and 26Articles of the Optional Protocol:2 and 5 (2) (b)The author of communication No. 3167/2018 is Johan Lets Pretorius, born in 1946 and the authors of communication No. 3218/2018 are his sons Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius, born in 1971 and 1977, respectively, all nationals of South Africa. The authors claim to be victims of a violation by the State Party of their rights under articles 9 (1), 10 (3), 12 (1-2), 14 (1-2), 14 (3) (b-e), 14 (5), 17 and 26 of the Covenant. The Optional Protocol entered into force for the State Party on 28 November 2002. The authors are represented by counsel.On 2 July 2018 (communication No. 3167/2018) and 19 March 2020 (communication No. 3218/2020), pursuant to rule 93 (1) of its rules of procedure, the Committee, acting through its Special Rapporteurs on new communications and interim measures denied the State party’s request to examine the admissibility of the communications separately from the merits. On 10 March 2026, pursuant to rule 97 (3) of the Committee’s rules of procedure, the Committee decided to join for a joint examination communications No. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018 in view of the substantial factual and legal similarity.Facts as submitted by the authors2.1Johan Lets Pretorius worked as a doctor with a medical practice in Potgietersrus Limpopo Province. Johan Pretorius also worked as a doctor and Wilhelm Pretorius as a preacher in the same town, until all three were arrested in 2002. They state that in view of the high criminality in the country, the white farming community in the countryside started to organise themselves for protection “in case there would be a general uprising of blacks against whites”. Protection was originally envisaged through a so called “commando system” that consisted of civilian reserves in the countryside. They state that the idea was self-protection and claim that self-protection requires one to be armed and note that this is legal in South Africa. 2.2The authors claim that the commando system (also named the Boeremag, or Boer force) was infiltrated by the security police who acted as provocateurs and “radicalised” members of the group. They further argue that “by and large” however, the whole process was closely monitored and steered by the security police until the first arrests were made in 2002.2.3The authors claim that the security police arbitrarily selected 23 persons and charged them with high treason, out of the hundreds of people who had attended the meetings of the so-called self-protection units, and that other meeting attendants were arbitrarily chosen as state witnesses. The defendants, among them the authors, were charged with 43 offences before the North Gauteng High Court, including high treason, terrorism, sabotage, one charge of murder, a charge of conspiracy to attempt to commit murder and various charges concerning the possession of explosives, illegal firearms and excessive ammunition. Johan Lets Pretorius was arrested on 15 September 2002 and was released on bail 18 months later. The main charge against him of high treason consisted of threats to overthrow the government. The authors claim that the threat to the State was “literally and figuratively a paper threat”. They state that it consisted of what was discussed, planned and written down in a document called document 12 in which a plan was outlined on how to take over the country by force. The authors claim that the plan was “unrealistic, sensational and a farce” and influenced by the security police agent. 2.4After the initial arrests of members of the units were made in 2002 Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius note that they “formed part of a group of men, after a war had been declared for the self-determination of the Boer people, namely the South African Boer Republic, who continued with the legitimate armed conflict”. They state that they saw themselves “as legitimate soldiers in a just armed conflict according to the Geneva Conventions (Protocol 1), for the liberation of the Boer people against a racist regime oppressing our people”. They planted several bombs in various locations. During one of the bombings, one woman was killed, and damage was caused to State property. Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius were arrested in December 2002, and they were detained until their sentencing in 2013. 2.5The authors claim that the trial against them was politically motivated and that the head investigator of Crime Intelligence was trying to make up for his previous actions against African National Congress (ANC) members for which he received amnesty in 2002 while he was investigating their case. They state that the investigator had previously been charged with eight counts of murder and seven counts of attempted murder of ANC members, as well as various other charges. They note that their trial was the most expensive and longest that has ever been held in the State Party.2.6On 29 October 2013, Johan Lets Pretorius was found guilty of high treason and sentenced to 30 years of imprisonment, of which 10 years were suspended. On the same date, Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius were found guilty of high treason and sentenced to 35 years of imprisonment of which ten years were suspended, five years for culpable homicide and eight years for conspiracy of attempted murder. The sentences were to be served concurrently. The authors note that their sentencing took place 11 years after their arrest in September and December 2002. Exhaustion of domestic remedies2.7The authors state that they in detail argued that their rights to a fair trial, a trial without undue delay, and the right to equality of arms had been violated in the proceedings before the trial court. It was emphasised before the trial court that it was the duty of the State Party to ensure that the trial was completed without undue delay, and that the prosecuting authority ignored this obligation when it joined more and more accused to the same trial, impacting negatively on each of the accused’s individual rights to a trial without undue delay. Even at the initial stages of the trial, counsel for some of the accused objected to the joining of additional accused and brought an application against the joinder, which was rejected by the trial court. It was pointed out during the trial that every time one of the accused exercised his procedural rights to cross-examine witnesses, it affected negatively on the right of other accused to a trial without unreasonable delay. The trial court and the prosecuting authority ignored these objections.2.8In December 2013 Johan Lets Pretorius applied for leave to appeal before the trial court. The appeal was limited to the factual basis of his conviction and sentence. The trial court refused the application for leave to appeal on 30 January 2014. In July 2016, Johan Lets Pretorius submitted a petition to the President of the Supreme Court of Appeal claiming that his right to have his conviction reviewed by a higher tribunal had been violated. He further claimed that his right to a fair trial had been violated due to: i) the length of the trial proceedings; ii) the effect the long trial had on his right to appeal; iii) the fact that his conviction was based on the testimony of accomplices, thus violating the principle of equality of arms; iv) the fact that he had been unrepresented during the testimony of a key state witness; v) the fact that his communication with counsel had been monitored during the trial; and vi) the fact that the composition of the trial court did not fulfil the requirements of an independent and impartial court established by law. The Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal however refused to accept the petition before the Supreme Court on the ground that the trial court judgement on conviction and sentence, the leave to appeal judgement and the trial record were not attached to the petition. The author claims that he had however not been provided with the court order of the trial court refusing his application for leave to appeal, or its judgment or record at the time of his petition before the Supreme Court. 2.9 After their conviction, Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius note that they attempted to obtain legal aid for the appeal process from the Legal Aid Board. However, no counsel was appointed for them. On 26 September 2016, the authors, unrepresented, submitted an application for leave to appeal before the trial court. The application was however dismissed by the trial court. After the dismissal of their leave to appeal application, the authors again applied for legal counsel to be appointed by the Legal Aid Board in order to petition the President of the Supreme Court of Appeal directly. After having failed to obtain the assistance of the Legal Aid Board the authors, unrepresented, submitted a petition before the President of the Supreme Court in March 2017 (the authors note that in their petition they raised the same grounds as set out in points i-vi in para. 2.8 above). The petition was not accepted by the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal because it did not contain the judgement on conviction and sentence of the trial court. The authors note that at the time of their petition in 2017 they had not received said judgements, but that in any case, as they were unrepresented, it was not a requirement under domestic law to submit the judgements together with their petition. 2.10The authors note that, at the time of the submission of their complaint before the Committee, five years had elapsed since their conviction and sentence by the High Court, and they argue that it is therefore unreasonable to continue with attempts to file petitions for leave to appeal. They further note that even if they were to obtain leave to appeal, the appeal process would last for a minimum of two years, bringing it to a conclusion 18 years after their arrest. They argue that to pursue any further domestic remedies would thus merely prolong their incarceration unreasonably. They note that a complaint may also be filed with the Constitutional Court. However, their request to be appointed a legal aid lawyer for filing such a petition was denied on 28 March 2018. They argue that even if financial aid to approach the Constitutional Court were to become available, and even if they were to get any legal relief from the Constitutional Court, the infringements of their rights have already occurred in view of the excessively long trial. Complaint Articles 9 (1), and 14 (1-2) – transport in arm-and-foot chains3.1 The authors claim that they were arbitrarily put in arm-and-foot chains when transported to the court while in detention, in violation of their right to security of person. The authors further claim that photos of them in chains were published widely and broadcasted on television. They claim that they were presented to the public as very dangerous criminals, or part of a group of dangerous criminals, amounting to a violation of their rights under article 14 (1-2) of the Covenant as this influenced the court’s impression of them. They further argue that the negative impression of them as dangerous was exacerbated by the fact that they were brought to the court in armoured vehicles with full blast sirens accompanied by heavily armed special force units with the presence of heavily armed police in the courtroom throughout the trial. They further claim that there is no procedure under South African law that prescribes transporting defendants in chains and that they could not complain to the court about the treatment as the court regarded it as a matter for the police.Articles 9 (1), 14 (1) and 26 – equality of arms3.2The authors note that, initially, the security police arrested other persons who had been involved in the same activities as they had. Only some of these persons were charged, while others were made state witnesses under section 204 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1977, with the rest released without charge. They claim that they were not informed about the reasons why they were chosen to be prosecuted, and why they were not given the opportunity to become state witnesses. They note that the persons who became state witnesses were granted immunity in return for their testimonies. They state that the trial court specifically recognised that there is no legal provision in domestic law that entitles an accused to be given any reasons why he was selected to be prosecuted or to be made a state witness. The authors argue that unfairness is inherent in section 204 of the Criminal Procedure Act as firstly, the prosecution has a bigger pool of witnesses available to it to prove its case because it can force an accomplice to testify by giving him or her immunity. Secondly, an accused’s right to call witnesses is limited by the provision as a person cannot be forced to testify in view of the prohibition on self-incrimination. Thirdly, a state witness is rewarded by being a satisfactory witness for the state by being granted immunity from prosecution. The authors claim that the selection of defendants and state witnesses was thus done arbitrarily in violation of their rights under articles 9 (1), 14 (1) and 26. Articles 14 (3) (c),14 (1-2) and 14 (5) – undue delay in proceedings and right to review 3.3The authors note that they were arrested in September and December 2002. The trial started on 19 May 2003. They claim that the prosecution kept joining accused to the trial against the objections of the defence counsels that this would prolong the trial. Ultimately 23 accused were joined to the trial and all charged with 43 offences. The prosecution called 158 witnesses and closed its case on 15 June 2007, over four years after the authors’ arrests. The authors state that the reason the prosecution joined so many accused in one trial was that it was allowed for under the Criminal Procedure Act and as it was necessary to prove the charge of conspiracy to commit an offence. Ultimately, however, the prosecution abandoned the conspiracy charges and only relied on direct evidence linking each individual to the alleged criminal acts of high treason. Johan Lets Pretorius additionally notes that with the exception of the charge of high treason, all the other charges against him were subsequently withdrawn. However, the fact that only the charge of high treason was going to be pursued became apparent only at the end of the trial, meaning that all the defendants were obliged during the whole length of the trial to tailor their defences to all the charges. The authors further note that the prosecution called 158 witnesses according to the trial court’s judgment but state that their conviction was however based on only 20 state witnesses (Johan Lets Pretorius) or 21 witnesses (Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius), despite this they had to attend court hearings of all the other state witnesses who were irrelevant for their cases.3.4The authors claim that the trial judge recognised that the Legal Aid Board, which is an organ of the state responsible for providing legal aid, played a significant role in the delay of the trial, especially in refusing to appoint legal representatives for some of the defendants. By the time the authors were sentenced in October 2013, 11 years had passed since their arrest. They further note that, at the time of the submission of their complaint in 2018, over 15 years had passed since their arrest and they had not yet managed to submit an appeal against their conviction, resulting in a violation of their right to be tried without undue delay. 3.5The authors further argue that the excessively long trial also violated the presumption of innocence under article 14 (2), especially as concerns Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius as they were detained for 11 years before they were sentenced. They argue that they were, therefore, prejudged as being guilty and deserving sentences of more than 10 years even before they were convicted, and that the other defendants likewise, also had to be sentenced to long prison sentences in order to justify the length of the proceedings. 3.6The authors also claim that the long trial violated their right to a fair trial and the right to review under articles 14 (1) and 14 (5), taking into account that at the time of submission of their complaint over 15 years had passed since their arrest and detention without them having been able to have their convictions and sentences reviewed by a higher tribunal. Concerning the right to appeal they further note that under domestic law a person convicted and sentenced by the High Court must apply to the trial judge for leave to appeal and if it is refused, he or she can petition the President of the Supreme Court of Appeal for leave to appeal. They note that the South African Criminal Procedure Act states explicitly that there is no right to appeal. They note that the trial judge and the Supreme Court of Appeal judges considering the petition have a very wide discretion whether or not to grant the necessary permission to appeal as the Act does not state the grounds according to which the discretion should be exercised, but contains merely the procedure to be followed to obtain the necessary permission for leave to appeal. The authors argue that the inherent discretion given to both the trial judge and the Supreme Court of Appeal to refuse leave to appeal is a clear violation of article 14 (5) of the Covenant.Articles 9 (1) and 12 (1-2) – right to liberty of movement3.7The authors further claim that the fact that they had to attend court sessions regularly (Johan Lets Pretorius) or the fact that they were detained throughout the trial (Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius) violated their right to liberty and security of person under article 9 (1). They also claim a violation of article 12 (1-2) as they could not travel freely in South Africa or choose their place of residence, because of bail conditions (Johan Lets Pretorius) and detention (Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius).Article 14(3)(d) and 14 (1) – presence at trial and lack of legal representation3.8Johan Lets Pretorius claims a violation of his rights under article 14 (3) (d) as he was not present during the testimony of a key witness for the prosecution. He argues that the fact that his counsel was present on this occasion is irrelevant for the consideration of his claim. 3.9Johan Lets Pretorius further claims that he was unrepresented for five months during the trial. After he could no longer afford a privately paid counsel, the Legal Aid Board took five months to appoint and pay his counsel. He claims that during the time he was unrepresented, key witnesses testified against him, including the testimony of one witness upon which his conviction was based. Additionally, as he suffers from hearing loss, he was unable to hear what the witnesses and counsels for the other defendants were saying. He further notes that the counsel the Legal Aid Board eventually appointed for him was also representing five other defendants in the same case without the Board having assessed whether there was a conflict of interest amongst the defendants. 3.10Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius claim that because of the inaction of the Legal Aid Board to provide them timely with legal counsel, they were unrepresented for one year and seven months during the trial. They were unrepresented during the cross-examination of key state witnesses, including testimonies by witnesses upon which their convictions were based. During this time, they were often not even in court while the hearings took place. They further note that they never had a counsel representing them individually, but had the same counsel or, as at the beginning of the trial, were grouped together with other defendants all represented by the same counsel. The authors claim that this amounts to a violation of their rights under article 14 (1) and (3) (d).Articles 14 (3) (b) and 17– right to legal privilege3.11The authors claim that their conversations with their legal representatives were monitored with both audio and visual surveillance during the proceedings. They state that an engineer, who installed the intercom system in the facilities they were being held, testified that they had the ability to listen in on consultations with counsel at any time. The authors note that objection was made to the trial court about the microphone system recording the consultations which took place in court, where they were forced by the police to consult with their legal representatives. In response the court only stated that it would look into the matter, but nothing was ever done and the consultations continued to be recorded. The authors further state that an ex-security police officer later confirmed at trial that all the cells, where consultations between legal representatives and accused sometimes occurred, as well as the consultation rooms in the court building, were monitored by the security police. The security police knew, and could see, everything that occurred in court between an accused and his legal representative. They then communicated the information immediately to the investigating officers present in the court, who communicated it to the prosecution. However, the trial court did not believe the witness and referred him for prosecution on account of perjury. Articles 9 (1) and 14 (1) – sentence by a court not established by law3.12The authors note that after their conviction, the trial judge declared the two assessors who had participated at the hearing functus officio. They state that under domestic law, the assessors are only part of a court until a conviction is rendered, and the judge alone is responsible for the sentencing process. The authors claim that despite this the trial judge kept one assessor on the bench while excusing the other one. They state that it was pointed out to the trial judge that the presence of one of the assessors on the bench might be problematic and raised questions as to undue influence. According to the trial judge the assessor was to help him with the facts. The authors claim that their sentencing was, therefore, in violation of article 14 (1) of the Covenant as the trial court’s composition was not based on law. Article 14 (1) – trial by an independent tribunal3.13The authors claim that the trial judge and at least one of the assessors in the case were former colleagues of the senior advocate of the prosecuting team, and that they had worked together in the same office under his leadership before the trial judge became a practising advocate and later a judge. They claim that the court was therefore not an independent and impartial tribunal in accordance with article 14 (1) of the Covenant.Article 10 (3) - sentence without regard to reformation and rehabilitation3.14The authors claim that the trial court only applied the principles of deterrence and retribution in sentencing them, without considering the principles of reformation and rehabilitation in violation of their rights under article 10 (3) of the Covenant.State Party’s observations on admissibility 4.1On 5 June 2018 the State Party submitted its observations on the admissibility of communication No. 3167/2018. The State party considers that the communication is inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. It notes that in his complaint the author indicates that he had petitioned the President of the Supreme Court. It considers that the author should have waited for a reply from the President of the Court before submitting his communication before the Committee. It further submits that if the author should disagree with the answer of the Supreme Court, he can also file a claim before the Constitutional Court. 4.2On 16 May 2019 the State Party submitted its observations on the admissibility of communication No. 3218/2018. It notes the authors’ claims that their trial was unduly delayed but argues that parts of these delays were attributable to the defendants’ requests for postponements of hearing sessions, including postponement requests made by the authors. The State Party further notes that the authors only proceeded with an application for leave to appeal of the trial court judgment two years and eight months after the conclusion of the hearing, while under the Criminal Procedure Act, this should have been done within 14 days of the judgment. The State Party further notes that the Registrar of the Supreme Court “indicated that once all the required documents are received, the petition will be considered” and that “it is to be noted that the National Prosecuting Authority is in possession of an electronic version of the record of proceedings and is in the process of obtaining the transcribed record, which is believed to be in the possession of the High Court”. The State Party argues that the authors would therefore be in position to proceed with an appeal process as soon as the required documents have been submitted to the Registrar of the Supreme Court. The State Party further notes that the authors have lodged four motion proceedings with the High Court, the latest of which was, at the time of its submission of its observations, to be heard in June 2019.Authors’ comments on the State Party’s observations on admissibility 5.1On 5 August and 31 October 2019, the authors submitted their comments on the State Party’s observations on admissibility. They note the State Party’s argument that it took the authors of communication No. 3218/2018 over two years to submit an application for leave to appeal. They reiterate their argument that they could not do so earlier as, despite numerous requests to the Legal Aid Board, they were not appointed counsel for the appeals proceeding. They further note the State Party’s argument that parts of the trial delays were due to defendants’ requests for postponements. They argue that the State Party has not provided any example of any alleged requests for postponement that it considered to be without merit and reiterate their argument that the trial proceeded even during periods when they were unrepresented. They note that the motion proceedings referred to by the State Party in its observations concerned only petitions for enforcement of basic prisoner rights, while the latest proceeding was a habeas corpus application based on their complaint before the Committee.5.2The authors further argue that they were unable to submit an effective appeal in their case within the designated statutory time limit referred to by the State Party in its observations. They note that the statutory time limit for an appeal of a High Court judgment in a criminal case is as follows: i) According to section 316 (1) of the Criminal Procedure Act of 1977 an accused may apply for leave to appeal to the trial judge within 14 days after the passing of the sentence, or within such extended period as the court may on application and for good cause shown, allow; ii) if such an application for leave to appeal is refused by the trial judge, the accused may according to section 316 (8) of the Criminal Procedure Act petition the President of the Supreme Court of Appeal for leave to appeal within 21 days after the trial judge’s refusal of leave to appeal, or within such extended period as may on application for good cause shown, be allowed; and iii) according to section 315 (4) of the Criminal Procedure Act there is no right to an automatic appeal of a High Court judgment, an appeal can only be submitted after an application or petition for leave to appeal has been granted, as stipulated in section 316 of the Act.5.3The authors note that their counsel at the time of their sentence regarded it as impossible to bring an effective appeal within the prescribed time or even thereafter due to the extensive trial record. Legal aid was not provided for an appeal, subsequent requests for legal aid to be provided were also denied by the Legal Aid Board. The authors argue that the delay in the bringing of the first application for leave to appeal to the High Court was not only caused by the extensive trial record and lack of legal representation, but also by the fact that they only got access to computers and the provisional court record in order to be able to compile an application for leave to appeal a year after their sentencing. This delay was exacerbated by the fact that their first application for leave to appeal was confiscated by officials of the Correctional Services Department when it was given to representatives of the Legal Aid Board for filing, which caused a further delay of nine months. Ultimately, counsel advised the authors pro bono on the legal grounds to bring an application for leave to appeal. These grounds were confined to legal grounds based primarily on the Criminal Procedure Act, the Constitution and the provisions of the Covenant. The application was heard by the trial judge on 26 September 2016. Condonation was given for the late application, but the leave to appeal was refused.5.4The authors had 21 days to petition the Supreme Court of Appeal for leave to appeal after their application was refused by the trial judge. However, they only received the record of the refused leave application by the trial court on 11 November 2016, that is, after the statutory time limit had already expired. They immediately thereafter began to compile their petition and gave it to the Legal Aid Board for filing early December 2016. The Legal Aid Board only filed it with the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal on 8 March 2017. It was the duty of the Registrar of the High Court to transmit the required documentation with the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal, however there is no record of this having been done. Although the Registrar of the High Court wrote to the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal on 31 March 2017 that he had sent the necessary documents to the Supreme Court, the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal wrote on 22 June 2017 to the authors that he had not received the judgment and sentence record and therefore refused to accept the petition. The authors note that at the time of the filings they had not received the official trial record of their case which is under the control of State Party authorities, neither in hard copy, nor in electronic form, despite numerous requests to the Legal Aid Board. They state that it was thus impossible for them to fulfil the requirement to submit said documentation in their petitions. They finally note that for the same reasons as set out above, their co-defendants were also unable to obtain leave to appeal, and the trial case was never reviewed by higher tribunal.Authors’ further submission6.On 21 October 2021 the authors provided further information on domestic proceedings. They note that in February 2019 they brought habeas corpus proceedings in the High Court for their permanent or temporary release based on the complaint submitted before the Committee. They state that the proceedings were based on two causes of action: i) The likely findings of the Committee of violations of the Covenant by the State Party in its conduct towards them; and ii) the violations of their right to appeal which occurred after the trial court in their case was functus officio and they were sentenced. On 22 November 2019 the High Court declined to exercise jurisdiction on the basis that it cannot review its own decision. After the dismissal of the application, the authors applied to the Supreme Court of Appeal for leave to appeal against the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court of Appeal dismissed the application without any reasons on 4 March 2021. The authors subsequently sought leave to appeal to the Constitutional Court of the decision by the Supreme Court. This application was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 22 September 2021, without reasons provided. The authors argue that they therefore tried their utmost not only to appeal their original convictions and sentences as is set out in their complaints to the Committee, but also to have another court adjudicate the violations of their rights as set out in the Constitution, to no avail.Lack of cooperation by the State Party 7.On 2 July 2018 (communication No. 3167/2018) and 19 March 2020 (communication No. 3218/2018) the State Party was informed that its request for the admissibility of the communications to be examined separately from the merits had been denied and it was requested to submit its observations on the merits of the communications. Reminders to the State Party to submit the observations on the merits were sent on 28 August 2019 (communication No. 3167/2018), 24 November 2021 (communication Nos. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018) and 30 January 2025 (communication Nos. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018). The Committee regrets the failure of the State Party to respond to these requests in a timely manner and to provide any information with regard to the merits of the authors’ claims. The Committee recalls that article 4 (2) of the Optional Protocol implicitly obliges States Parties to examine in good faith all allegations brought against them and to make available to the Committee all the information at their disposal. In the absence of a reply from the State Party, due weight must be given to the authors’ allegations, to the extent that they are substantiated.Issues and proceedings before the CommitteeConsideration of admissibility8.1Before considering any claims contained in a communication, the Committee must decide, in accordance with rule 97 of its rules of procedure, whether the communication is admissible under the Optional Protocol.8.2The Committee has ascertained, as required under article 5 (2) (a) of the Optional Protocol, that the same matter is not being examined under another procedure of international investigation or settlement. 8.3The Committee notes the State Party’s submission that the communications should be found inadmissible under article 5 (2) (b) of the Optional Protocol for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. It notes the authors’ argument that after their convictions they submitted applications for leave to appeal before the trial court as stipulated under domestic law, and that following the rejection of said applications, they submitted petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal. It further notes their argument that considering the lengthy trial, the proceedings in their case have also been unduly prolonged.8.4The Committee recalls its jurisprudence that, although there is no obligation to exhaust domestic remedies if they have no chance of being successful or if the application of remedies is unreasonably prolonged, authors of communications must exercise due diligence in the pursuit of available remedies, and that mere doubts or assumptions about their effectiveness do not absolve the authors from exhausting them. 8.5In the present case the Committee notes that following their conviction and sentencing all three authors made applications for leave to appeal to the trial court, which rejected their applications on 30 January 2014 (communication No. 3167/2018) and 26 September 2016 (communication No. 3218/2018). The Committee notes the State Party’s argument that the applications for leave to appeal by Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius was filed over two years after their sentencing, thus failing to meet the deadline of filing an application for leave to appeal within 14 days of the judgment as stipulated in the Criminal Procedure Act. The Committee however notes the authors’ undisputed argument that the trial court excused the late filing of the application. The Committee further notes that following the rejection by the trial court of their applications for leave to appeal, all three authors submitted petitions to the Supreme Court of Appeal containing their claims of fair trial violations (see paras. 2.8-2.9). The Committee notes the authors’ information that the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal refused to accept the petition by Johan Lets Pretorius on the ground that the trial judgement on conviction and sentence, the leave to appeal judgement and the trial record were not attached to the petition and their information that the Registrar refused the petition by Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius as it did not contain the judgement on conviction and sentence of the trial court. The Committee further notes the authors’ unrefuted argument that it was not possible to submit said documents together with their petition, as at the time of the submission of the petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal they had not received the documentation from the trial court, and that in the case of Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius who were unrepresented, it was additionally not a requirement under domestic law to submit said documents together with the petition. 8.6The Committee further notes the State Party’s submission that the authors could also have filed claims before the Constitutional Court. It notes the authors’ argument that their request to be appointed a legal aid lawyer for filing such a petition was denied on 28 March 2018 and their argument that the infringements of their rights had already occurred in view of the excessively long trial. The Committee further notes that the State Party has not provided any further information on the possibility in the authors case to obtain a remedy from the Constitutional Court to address their claims, following the rejection of their applications for leave to appeal. Taking into account the authors’ information on the attempts made to exhaust domestic remedies by submitting applications for leave to appeal before the trial court and by filing petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal, as well as taking into account the fact, that by the time the authors’ petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal were rejected in 2016 and 2017, 13 years had elapsed since their arrest, the Committee considers that it is not precluded by article 5 (2) (b) of the Optional Protocol from considering the present communication.8.7The Committee notes the authors’ claim that their rights under article 9 (1) and 14 (1-2) of the Covenant were violated as they were transported to the court hearings in arm-and-foot chains, and as photos of them in chains were published in media, thus presenting them as dangerous criminals. It further notes their claims that the excessively long trial also violated the presumption of innocence under article 14 (2), as considering their long periods of detention they were prejudged as being guilty. The Committee also notes the authors’ claims that the selection of defendants and state witnesses was done arbitrarily in violation of their rights under articles 9 (1), 14 (1) and 26. The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that the trial court in sentencing them failed to take into account the principles of reformation and rehabilitation in violation of their rights under article 10 (3) of the Covenant. The Committee however considers that the authors have not sufficiently substantiated these claims, and it therefore finds the claims inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.8The Committee notes the authors’ claims that the fact that they had to attend court sessions regularly or the fact that they were detained throughout the trial violated their right to liberty and security of person under article 9 (1), as well as their claim that their rights under article 12 (1-2) were violated as they could not travel freely or choose their place of residence during the trial. In the absence of any further specific information or argumentation as to said claims, the Committee finds the claims to be insufficiently substantiated for the purposes of admissibility and inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.9The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that their rights under articles 9 (1) and 14 (1) were violated as the trial court’s composition was not based in law and as the trial judge and one of the assessors in the hearing were former colleagues of the senior advocate of the prosecuting team. The Committee however notes that the authors have not provided any further specific information or argumentation in support of these claims, and it therefore finds the claims to be insufficiently substantiated for the purposes of admissibility and inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.10The Committee however considers that the authors have sufficiently substantiated the remaining claims on: their right to be present at trial; their lack of legal representation; the undue delay in proceedings; the right to review; and the right to confidential communication with counsel, for the purposes of admissibility. Accordingly, the Committee declares the authors’ claims under articles 14 (3) (b), (c), (d), 14 (5) and 17 of the Covenant admissible and proceeds with its consideration of the merits.Consideration of the merits 9.1The Committee has considered the communication in the light of all the information submitted to it by the parties, in accordance with article 5 (1) of the Optional Protocol. The Committee notes that, in failing to respond to a communication, or responding incompletely, a State that is the object of a communication puts itself at a disadvantage because the Committee is then compelled to consider the communication in the absence of full information relating to the communication. In the absence of any explanations from the State Party in respect of the merits, due weight must be given to the author’s allegations to the extent that they have been sufficiently substantiated (see para. 7 above).9.2The Committee notes the authors’ claims that their rights under article 14 (3) (d) of the Covenant were violated as they were not present during parts of the trial, were unrepresented during periods of the trial, and were not appointed counsel representing them individually. The Committee recalls that article 14 (3) (d) guarantees the right of the accused person to be tried in his or her presence and to have legal assistance assigned to him or her whenever the interests of justice so require, and without payment by them in any such case if they do not have sufficient means for such payment. The Committee further recalls that the gravity of the offence is important in deciding whether counsel should be assigned “in the interest of justice” as is the existence of some objective chance of success at the appeals stage. 9.3In the present case, concerning the gravity of the offences in question, the Committee notes that the authors were on trial for serious criminal charges, facing long periods of imprisonment if convicted. The Committee notes the authors’ claims that they were not present at parts of the trial, including testimonies by key witnesses. It further notes their claims that they were unrepresented for periods of five months (communication No. 3167/2018) and one year and seven months (communication No. 3218/2018), including during testimonies of witnesses upon which their convictions were based. The Committee finally notes their claims that counsel eventually appointed for them through the Legal Aid Board also represented other defendants in the case without the Board having assessed whether there was a conflict of interest amongst the defendants (see paras. 3.8-3.10). The Committee notes that the State Party has not submitted any observations on the merits of the present communication or refuted any of the authors’ claims. In the absence of a response from the State Party in that regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims that they were not present at parts of the trial, were unrepresented during crucial periods of the trial, and that there was no assessment made as to whether there was a conflict of interest among defendants represented by the same counsel appointed to them, thus amounting to a violation of the authors’ rights under article 14 (3) (d) of the Covenant.9.4The Committee notes the authors’ claim that their right under article 14 (3) (c) to be tried without undue delay was violated, as by the time they were sentenced at first instance in October 2013, 11 years had passed since their arrests in September and December 2002. The Committee recalls that the right of the accused to be tried without undue delay is not only designed to avoid keeping persons too long in a state of uncertainty about their fate and, if held in detention during the period of the trial, to ensure that such deprivation of liberty does not last longer than necessary in the circumstances of the specific case, but also to serve the interests of justice. What is reasonable has to be assessed in the circumstances of each case, taking into account mainly the complexity of the case, the conduct of the accused, and the manner in which the matter was dealt with by the administrative and judicial authorities. In cases where the accused are denied bail by the court, they must be tried as expeditiously as possible. The Committee further recalls that this guarantee relates not only to the time between the formal charging of the accused and the time by which a trial should commence, but also the time until the final judgement on appeal. All stages, whether in first instance or on appeal must take place without undue delay.9.5In the present case the Committee notes the authors’ argument that their trial at first instance lasted 11 years, with two of the authors detained during this period. It notes the State Party’s argument that parts of the delays were attributable to the defendants’ requests for postponements of hearing sessions, including postponement requests made by the authors. The Committee however notes the authors’ argument that the State Party has not provided any example of any alleged requests for postponement made by them that it considered to be without merit. It further notes their arguments that the trial was delayed as accused were joined to the same trial despite counsels’ objection that this would unduly prolong the trial and their argument that the delays were partly caused by delays by the Legal Aid Board in appointing legal representatives for some of the defendants. In the absence of any further explanation by the State Party regarding the excessive length of the trial, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (3) (c) of the Covenant.9.6The Committee further notes the authors’ claim that their rights under article 14 (5) of the Covenant were violated as they were unable to have their convictions and sentences reviewed by a higher tribunal. The Committee recalls that the right to have one’s conviction and sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal imposes on the State Party a duty to review substantively, both on the basis of sufficiency of the evidence and of the law, the conviction and sentence, such that the procedure allows for due consideration of the nature of the case. A review that is limited to the formal or legal aspects of the conviction without any consideration whatsoever of the facts is not sufficient under the Covenant. The Committee further recalls that the right to have one’s conviction reviewed can only be exercised effectively if the convicted person is entitled to have access to a duly reasoned, written judgement of the trial court, and, at least in the court of first appeal where domestic law provides for several instances of appeal, also to other documents, such as trial transcripts, necessary to enjoy the effective exercise of the right to appeal.9.7In the present case, the Committee notes the authors’ argument that at the time of the submission of their complaint before the Committee over 15 years had passed since their arrest and detention without them having been able to have their convictions and sentences reviewed by a higher tribunal. It notes their information that after their applications for leave to appeal before the trial court had been rejected, they submitted petitions to the Supreme Court of Appeal which were refused on the ground that documentation such as the trial judgement on conviction and sentence, the leave to appeal judgement and the trial record were not attached to the petition. The Committee further notes the authors’ argument that it was not possible for them to submit said documents, as at the time of the submission of the petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal they had not received the requested documentation. The Committee thus notes the authors’ submission that despite attempts to have their conviction and sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal, their appeals were rejected without any consideration of the facts in their case or review of the claims raised by them concerning fair trial violations. In the absence of any explanation by the State Party in this regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (5) of the Covenant.9.8The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that their conversations with their legal representatives were monitored with both audio and visual surveillance during the court proceedings. The Committee recalls that the right to communicate with counsel requires that counsel should be able to meet their clients in private and to communicate with the accused in conditions that fully respect the confidentiality of their communications. In the present case the Committee notes the authors’ claims that the court microphone system recorded consultations between defendants and counsel which took place in court, that their cells, where consultations between legal representatives and defendants sometimes occurred were monitored, as well as their claim that the consultation rooms in the court building were monitored. In the absence of any submission by the State Party refuting the authors’ claims in this regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (3) (b) of the Covenant. Having thus concluded, the Committee will not separately consider the same claims raised by the authors under article 17 of the Covenant.10. The Committee, acting under article 5 (4) of the Optional Protocol, is of the view that the facts before it disclose a violation of the authors’ rights under articles 14 (3) (b), (c) and (d) and 14 (5) of the Covenant. 11. Pursuant to article 2 (3) (a) of the Covenant, the State Party is under an obligation to provide the authors with an effective remedy. This requires it to make full reparation to individuals whose Covenant rights have been violated. The Committee considers that, in the present case, its Views on the merits of the complaint constitute sufficient reparation for the violations found. The State Party is also under an obligation to take steps to prevent similar violations occurring in the future. 12. Bearing in mind that, by becoming a party to the Optional Protocol, the State Party has recognized the competence of the Committee to determine whether there has been a violation of the Covenant and that, pursuant to article 2 of the Covenant, the State Party has undertaken to ensure to all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction the rights recognized in the Covenant and to provide an effective remedy when it has been determined that a violation has occurred, the Committee wishes to receive from the State Party, within 180 days, information about the measures taken to give effect to the Committee’s Views. The State Party is also requested to publish the present Views and to have them widely disseminated in the languages of the State Party. __________________________
